column86: Strict notice required, then particulars and monthly updates.
column87: Potential cost/time only if claim compliant.
column88: Potential EOT if critical path delayed.
column89: Keep request dates, required-by dates, late response proof, and critical path analysis.

column83: Employer gives site access under contract conditions.
column84: Access is entitlement-sensitive: if the Contractor cannot work because access is not given, it can be strong, but only with proof of readiness and criticality.
column86: Immediate notice if access not available.
column87: Possible cost if proven and not excluded.
column88: Possible EOT if critical access denied.
column89: Keep handover records, photographs, readiness evidence, and programme logic.

column83: Authority permits/licenses are excluded from Accepted Contract Amount, but responsibilities depend on the specific permit and law.
column84: This is a possible variation/claim zone, but not a blanket excuse for slow authority processing.
column86: Notify authority delay and cost as soon as known.
column87: Recoverable if Employer-risk or excluded cost instructed/required.
column88: Possible EOT if authority issue blocks critical work and Contractor acted diligently.
column89: Keep applications, authority receipts, correspondence, and delay chronology.

column83: Engineer administers instructions and determinations under the Contract.
column84: Engineer decisions are central evidence. Silence or informal site discussion is weaker than written instruction/determination.
column86: Ask for written instruction/determination where impact exists.
column87: Payment depends on formal valuation/determination.
column88: Delay depends on accepted programme impact.
column89: Convert verbal directions into written confirmation immediately.

column83: Contractor must execute, complete, and remedy defects in accordance with the Contract and good practice.
column84: Broad duty means Contractor carries coordination, means, methods, and completion risk unless a clause shifts it.
column86: Notify only where Employer-risk event prevents performance.
column87: Defects/rework usually Contractor cost.
column88: Contractor-caused delay not excusable.
column89: Keep method statements, approvals, inspection records, and defect closure evidence.

column83: Contractor must verify and review design documents as required by the Contract.
column84: Failure to review early can make later design objections look like Contractor delay or late discovery.
column86: Raise design issues promptly and before affected works.
column87: Late design comments may not justify extra cost.
column88: Late review can delay shop drawings/procurement.
column89: Maintain design review log, consultant reports, RFIs, and dates.

column83: Contractor must cooperate with other contractors and anticipate simultaneous work.
column84: Minor disruption, sequencing changes, and interface inconvenience may already be priced and programmed.
column86: Only substantial, critical, Employer-caused interference should be claimed.
column87: Minor interface cost likely unrecoverable.
column88: Minor resequencing likely no EOT.
column89: Keep interface meeting minutes, obstruction logs, photos, and critical path proof.

column83: Unexpected physical conditions may support entitlement if properly notified and proven.
column84: Site difficulty alone is not enough. Contractor must show unforeseeability, impact, and compliance with notice rules.
column86: Immediate notice before disturbing evidence where possible.
column87: Possible cost if conditions qualify.
column88: Possible EOT if critical path affected.
column89: Preserve photos, survey, test reports, expert opinion, and baseline assumptions.

column83: Utilities relocation/protection is excluded from price, but Contractor must manage site utilities obligations carefully.
column84: Utility events can be claimable if outside scope, but damage or poor protection can become Contractor liability.
column86: Notify conflict/damage immediately and follow variation/claim procedure.
column87: Potential extra for instructed protection/relocation; liability if Contractor damages utilities.
column88: Potential EOT if utility issue blocks critical work and not Contractor fault.
column89: Keep utility drawings, trial pit records, permits, photos, and incident reports.

column83: Employer-supplied items, especially steel as part of advance, depend on approved programme and requisition process.
column84: A steel delay claim needs proof that Contractor requested correctly, was ready to use it, and the delay hit critical path.
column86: Notice immediately if free issue material is late, defective, or short.
column87: May affect payment/advance and possible prolongation.
column88: Possible EOT if critical and not Contractor-caused.
column89: Keep approved programme, requisitions, delivery notes, stock records, and activity impacts.

column83: Daily, weekly, and monthly reports must include progress, delay analysis, programme update, logs, photos, procurement, submittals, quality, and pending issues.
column84: Reports are not paperwork only. They become the project record for delay, payment, and claim proof.
column86: Monthly claim/variation account must be separate and up to date.
column87: Weak reports weaken IPCs and claims.
column88: Weak reports weaken delay analysis.
column89: Submit complete reports and reconcile them with notices, programme updates, and IPCs.

column83: Contractor must submit shop drawings, as-built drawings, and source files where required.
column84: Late or incomplete drawings can stop approvals, inspections, and taking-over.
column86: Follow submittal timing and resubmission period.
column87: Rework/correction generally Contractor cost.
column88: Can become Contractor delay if on critical path.
column89: Maintain drawing register, revision history, approvals, and transmittals.

column83: If Contractor fails to submit or obtain approval of QMS, Employer/RFP quality plan may be deemed final.
column84: Contractor loses control over the quality framework if its own plan is late or rejected.
column86: QMS details due early after commencement.
column87: Noncompliance can lead to rejected work and withheld approvals.
column88: Rejected IRs/NCRs can delay progress and taking-over.
column89: Submit QMS, QC manager approval, ITPs, NCR logs, and corrective action records.

column83: If Contractor fails to submit or approve HSE plan, Employer/RFP safety plan may govern.
column84: Safety noncompliance can stop work and still remain Contractor risk.
column86: Submit HSE plan and incident reports on time.
column87: Stop-work or corrective measures may be Contractor cost.
column88: Safety stoppages can delay works without EOT if Contractor fault.
column89: Keep HSE plan, inductions, toolbox talks, PPE logs, accident reports, and close-outs.

column83: Key Contractor personnel require approval and compliance with contract requirements.
column84: Changing or lacking approved staff can be treated as management noncompliance and used against progress claims.
column86: Notify changes and obtain approvals.
column87: May affect payment/certification indirectly.
column88: Weak staffing undermines EOT defenses.
column89: Keep CV approvals, org chart, attendance, and replacement approvals.

column83: Programme must be P6, resource/cost/cash loaded, with narratives, long lead items, free issue materials, and other contractors' milestones.
column84: A simple bar chart is not enough. Without a compliant baseline/update, delay claims become much harder to prove.
column86: Programme submission and monthly update deadlines matter.
column87: IPC, cash flow, and delay claims depend on programme quality.
column88: Critical path proof depends on accepted logic.
column89: Keep baseline, updates, narratives, calendars, resources, cash flow, and change logs.

column83: If delay reaches 10 percent of remaining calendar days or at least 45 days, Contractor must submit recovery plan within 28 days.
column84: The contract creates an early warning and acceleration pressure mechanism before final delay damages.
column86: Recovery plan due within 28 days after update showing delay.
column87: Recovery may be Contractor cost if delay is Contractor risk.
column88: Failure worsens delay exposure.
column89: Submit recovery plan with manpower, shifts, resequencing, procurement, and float recovery.

column83: EOT is available only for qualifying events and compliant claims.
column84: Even a real Employer-caused delay can be lost if notice, particulars, monthly updates, or critical path proof are missing.
column86: Strict claim notice and monthly account requirements.
column87: Prolongation cost depends on entitlement and concurrency rules.
column88: EOT protects against delay damages if proven.
column89: Maintain delay event register, notices, particulars, updates, and delay analysis.

column83: If progress is too slow, Contractor may be required to revise methods or accelerate.
column84: If the delay is Contractor-caused, recovery is usually at Contractor cost.
column86: Respond quickly to slow-progress notices.
column87: Additional resources may not be payable.
column88: Recovery obligations can change sequence and productivity.
column89: Keep productivity records and separate Contractor delay from Employer delay.

column83: Engineer/Employer may instruct suspension under contract conditions.
column84: Suspension can be entitlement-bearing if not Contractor fault, but must be documented precisely.
column86: Notice/claim immediately after suspension instruction and resumption.
column87: Possible cost if compensable under contract.
column88: Possible EOT if critical path affected.
column89: Keep suspension instruction, affected resources, idle plant/labour, and restart records.

column81: Tests on completion and failed tests
column83: Failure to pass tests can trigger remedial obligations and retesting.
column84: Testing failure usually shifts time/cost risk back to Contractor unless caused by Employer design/instruction.
column86: Notify cause if failure not Contractor fault.
column87: Retesting/remedial cost likely Contractor risk.
column88: Failed tests delay taking-over.
column89: Keep test plans, results, calibration, causes, corrective works, and retest approvals.

column83: Taking-over requires substantial completion and conditions such as no rejected IRs, no open NCRs, clear site limits, debris removal, and safe access.
column84: Physical completion is not enough. Paperwork, NCRs, housekeeping, and safe access can block TOC and retention release.
column86: Apply for TOC only with supporting close-out evidence.
column87: Retention release and final payment depend on TOC.
column88: Delay damages risk continues until TOC/completion accepted.
column89: Prepare TOC dossier, NCR closeout, as-builts, test certificates, and site clearance evidence.

column83: DNP is 365 days and Contractor must remedy defects.
column84: The project is not commercially finished at TOC. Defects affect final retention and final certificate.
column86: Respond to defect notices promptly.
column87: Unremedied defects may be deducted or completed by others.
column88: Defects can delay final release.
column89: Maintain defect register, response dates, repair records, and Engineer acceptance.
